But since you do seem willing to listen: interest rates are a requirement for any kind of functional economy. They provide an incentive for people to loan out their excess wealth to investors, who provide that wealth to entrepreneurs looking to start new businesses and grow the economy. Without interest rates, there's no incentive for people to risk their excess capital on uncertain endeavors, and entrepreneurs are forced to rely almost exclusively on their personal funds to start businesses, bringing economic activity to a near standstill. In general, neither "high" nor "low" interest rates are good, what you really want is for interest rates to be determined by the market--the relative supply and demand for loanable funds will determine what the appropriate interest rate is for the market at the time, depending on how many people are looking to borrow, how many people have have money to loan out, how much the borrowers are asking for, and how much the lenders have available. Lower interest rates signal that there's a greater quantity of loanable funds available, and makes it more desirable for entrepreneurs to invest in future production rather than present production. Higher interest rates signal that there's a smaller amount of loanable funds available, and makes it more desirable for entrepreneurs to maximize present production rather than investing in future production.

But in our current economy, interest rates are not set by the market. They're set somewhat arbitrarily by the Federal Reserve, and the value is always either above or below the market-clearing price. Most often, the Federal Reserve seeks to keep interest rates artificially low. Artificially low interest rates make it appear as if there's a lot more capital available than there really is, and implies that there's going to be a future increase in production. If interest rates were low because of market forces this would be the case, and there would be no issue. But interest rates are not low because of market forces, they're low becasue the Fed has willed it to be so. As a result, there aren't nearly enough loanable funds in the market as the interest rate implies, and the expected future growth never happens. This means that many of the investments that were made with the cheap credit from the low interest don't turn a profit. Businesses fail en mass, capital is sold off, and employees are laid off because the expected increase in consumption never came, and the economy begins to painfully normalize as all of these nonproductive assets are liquidated. You probably recognize what I'm describing as an economic recession. Contrary to Keynesian rhetoric, artificially low interest rates, or some other form of systematic credit expansion, have been the cause of every recession to date, and this makes low interest rates very undesirable.

Higher interest rates aren't exactly "good"--they do slow the rate of investment, and make consumption loans more expensive. But they don't cause systematic crashes of the economy, they don't whet the federal government's appetite for money-printing the way low interest rates do (the way the Fed decreases interest rates is by increasing the money supply, i.e. creating new currency, i.e. money-printing), and they reward those people who have deferred their gratification by saving their money instead of spending it all. Investors and entrepreneurs are of course inconvenienced, but that's preferable to the alternative.
